verdict.reasoning: Patient says he is “kind of struggling to breathe at the moment” and “potentially there's a bit of swelling in my lips and tongue. Feels a bit weird” after “I got stung by a wasp recently…It was just a few minutes ago.”
When asked when the sting occurred, patient states, “It was just a few minutes ago,” and location is confirmed as “Yeah, it was on my arm.”
Patient and clinician describe “a bit of a rash on my arm” and later “It's slightly red…there's a bit of a…like a hole where…I think that the…Yes. Yeah. The puncture mark.”
Patient describes the area as “just a bit. Kind of blotchy and a bit of a rash.”
When asked about swelling, clinician says “Is there any swelling around that area that you can see? I couldn't see any.” Patient replies, “Not particularly…It doesn't feel like particularly swollen.”

Initially patient reports difficulty breathing: “I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment,” but later clarifies, “I don't feel like it's like particularly acute…I'm just kind of a bit anxious.” Clinician notes “Your breathing seems all right to me right now.”
Patient states, “I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse. I just wanted to speak to someone.”
In past medical history, patient says, “I've had eczema before. That's kind of the…The major thing.”
Patient answers, “Yeah, sometimes. Occasionally,” to “do you suffer from anxiety or panic attacks,” and then “Have you ever been on medication for that? – No. No.”
When asked, “Have you got a history of anaphylaxis?” patient replies, “Not that I know of, no.”
To “Have you got a history of any allergies to anything?” patient responds, “I'm allergic to penicillin.”
In social history, patient states, “I am a computer scientist.”
Patient answers “Yes” when asked, “And you're living alone?”
Patient confirms, “I have a cat,” when asked about pets at home.
Patient denies pet and food allergies: “Not that I know of. Yeah, I've been around dogs and cats,” and “And you've got no food allergies as far as you're aware? – No.”

Clinician comments that breathing seems okay and conducts conversation normally; patient is able to answer in full sentences with no mention of speech difficulty: “Your breathing seems all right to me right now…based on how you look, how you're talking to me and how you're breathing…”
Clinician notes, “your lips don't seem swollen to me right now,” after visually assessing them via video.

After mouth/throat inspection, clinician reassures, “what I'd be worried about…is…any swelling of the lips or the tissues inside the mouth…the soft tissues of the airway…Thankfully, I can't see any of that right now.”
Clinician notes normal speech: “based on how you look, how you're talking to me and how you're breathing,” and asks patient to say “ah,” which he does appropriately, indicating normal phonation.

Clinician repeatedly observes normal breathing: “Your breathing seems all right to me right now” and later, “based on…how you're breathing… I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction.”

Exam description: “That looks okay to me. Right now. Does it look red to you…? – It's slightly red…And…The puncture mark… Now, is there any swelling around that area…? I couldn't see any. – Not particularly…It doesn't feel like particularly swollen.”
No vital signs (e.g., BP, HR, RR, temp, SpO2) are mentioned anywhere in the transcript, so stating they were not obtained is consistent with the record.

Clinician concludes, “I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction…It seems to me that this is a localized allergic reaction…Given that it hasn't happened initially, it's unlikely to happen later,” after a wasp/bee sting minutes before with mild redness and no airway signs.
Patient expresses anxiety, and clinician acknowledges: “I can understand it is quite anxiety provoking…Sometimes a chat is all you need to calm things down,” indicating anxiety related to the sting.

Clinician advises, “try and take some antihistamines…you can get pyritone or chlorphenamine and you can take one tablet, four milligrams, up to about six times a day. Okay? Or you can just take a one a day.”

Clinician instructs, “if anything changes, if anything deteriorates, either make an appointment with us or go straight to ae…for example, you would have swelling of the lips, difficulty breathing, you might have something called stridor…if it's progressing rapidly, it's better to go straight to AE…”
Clinician states, “If the redness in your arm spreads and it feels hot or, you know, you have signs of any localised infection, we may need to think about other treatments like an antibiotic.”

Clinician says, “on the basis of what you told me, I don't think you need any allergy testing…However, if it was to happen that…you're having these kind of reactions on a regular basis or other non specific rashes, you might need to think about blood testing. I don't think we're at that moment yet.”

Clinician plans, “I'm going to leave some information about anaphylactic reactions just for you to read about it…Get back to us if you're feeling worried. Just have a low threshold for having a chat with us.”
